result: {"decisions":[{"item_type":"advice","point":"D2","problem":"How to find the main causes of COVID-19 transmission and which protective measures work.","did":"Argues every country should run many studies and RCTs on transmission causes and PPE, using lockdown conditions and settings like hospitals and care homes.","alternatives_named":[],"stated_reason":"Under lockdown it is easier to attribute infections to a cause, and hospitals and care homes are numerous.","quote":"Under lockdown, it should be much easier to work out the cause of infection. There are also enormous numbers of hospitals and large care homes all around the world (E.g. janitors and cleaners would seem higher risk if surfaces/aerosol is a major mode of transmission.)","source":"C1"},{"item_type":"advice","point":"D2","problem":"How to test whether indoor versus outdoor settings change infection risk using existing data.","did":"Suggests comparing infection rates by job (indoor vs. outdoor) under lockdown, and comparing houses with and without gardens in the same area.","alternatives_named":[],"stated_reason":"Under lockdown most infections will come from work, so job type is a usable natural comparison.","quote":"Under lockdown, most infections will be from work. So compare indoor vs. outdoor jobs. (What about houses with gardens/decks vs. not in the same area, in a place where the weather is nice in March/April?)","source":"C1"},{"item_type":"advice","point":"D1","problem":"Why only some people with similar exposure at superspreader events get infected.","did":"Proposes investigating variance in infectability, including whether it is general or person-specific, using the superspreader case studies.","alternatives_named":["randomness in droplets"],"stated_reason":"Many people with very similar exposure, such as 50% in the Korean call center, were not infected, which randomness alone is unlikely to explain.","quote":"But I'd a substantial part of this is variance in infectability. Are some people less infectable in general, or just relative to a particular person?","source":"C1"},{"item_type":"disagreement","point":"D5","problem":"Whether the absence of second waves in hard-hit places shows herd immunity is doing a lot of work.","did":"Questions the herd immunity explanation and points to mobility data and behavior changes in places with a strong first wave.","alternatives_named":["herd immunity as the main explanation"],"stated_reason":"Hard-hit places kept mobility low and adopted distancing and masking, and he sees no good evidence that herd immunity plays more than the expected 15-30% reduction in R.","quote":"Have you looked at the mobility data? Most (maybe all) of the places in Europe that had a strong first wave kept mobility low (esp. public transport and workplace) and have adopted strict social distancing in public spaces and some level of masking.","source":"C3"},{"item_type":"disagreement","point":"D2","problem":"Whether mobility and contact data are valid proxies for risk when comparing places with and without big first waves.","did":"Defends mobility and contact-survey proxies as predictive of spread and proposes using them to compare predicted contact across cities.","alternatives_named":["dismissing mobility data as poorly correlated with risk taken"],"stated_reason":"Published papers have used these proxies to model cases and deaths successfully.","quote":"The point is that we know you can predict spread using these proxies for contact. So you can actually see if the amount of predicted contact is lower in NYC, London, Madrid and Lombardy vs. places that didn't have a big first wave","source":"C5"},{"item_type":"disagreement","point":"D5","problem":"Whether Sweden's containment without formal lockdown is a mystery needing a special explanation.","did":"Explains Sweden's outcome by voluntary behavior change in response to neighbors' tighter restrictions and lower death tolls, so he sees no mystery.","alternatives_named":["treating Sweden as an unexplained control group"],"stated_reason":"Public transit use and cinema visits dropped substantially in Sweden even without a formal lockdown.","quote":"Without a formal lockdown, there was a huge change of behavior in Sweden. I'd guess Swedes were aware that all the countries around them had tighter restrictions and much lower death tolls. So they acted to reduce risk.","source":"C5"},{"item_type":"advice","point":"D6","problem":"Whether available data can support conclusions about household transmission by relationship type.","did":"Declines to draw a strong conclusion about spouses vs. other household members, citing limited data that mostly comes from certain countries.","alternatives_named":[],"stated_reason":"Few studies distinguish relationships, and the data come mostly from China, Korea and Taiwan, where households are mostly nuclear or extended families.","quote":"I don't think there's enough data to draw a strong empirical conclusion. Most of our data for estimating SAR is from China/Korea/Taiwan and I'd guess these are mostly nuclear families or extended family (not many group house / flatmates).","source":"C6"},{"item_type":"disagreement","point":"D5","problem":"How to interpret the seemingly low household secondary attack rate.","did":"Argues the low rate is not surprising, given overdispersion in infectiousness, so many infected people infect no one.","alternatives_named":["treating the low household infection rate as shocking"],"stated_reason":"If a minority of people cause most infections, many infected people are barely infectious even at close contact.","quote":"There is probably some overdispersion. Say 20% of people do 60-80% of all infecting. So many people cause zero new infections. I'd presume such people just aren't very infectious and so even if they spend a lot of time with household members they won't infect them.","source":"C7"},{"item_type":"advice","point":"D3","problem":"Whether to accept a sweeping claim about engineering careers and regulation stifling innovation without supporting evidence.","did":"Asks for actual data rather than accepting the claim, and notes counter-data on engineer salaries.","alternatives_named":["accepting the claim on rhetoric"],"stated_reason":"Salary data show non-software engineers did not fare much worse, and the claim was backed only by assertion.","quote":"Not to say regulation doesn't limit innovation, but I'd want to see actual data on this and not just bluster.","source":"C8"},{"item_type":"decision","point":"D5","problem":"Whether evidence supports surface (fomite) transmission of COVID-19, which a commenter was doubting.","did":"Cites a detailed hospital outbreak investigation as good evidence of indirect contact transmission, while limiting what it implies about everyday risks like deliveries.","alternatives_named":["concluding surface transmission is negligible"],"stated_reason":"The spatial pattern of infections in the South African hospital outbreak pointed to indirect contact via health care workers or fomites.","quote":"A detailed investigation of outbreak in a South African hospital found pretty good evidence for transmission by surfaces or indirect contact (nurse touches infected person A and then later touches susceptible person B). Doesn't mean risk from deliveries is significant but worth being wary of surfaces in general.","source":"C2"}]}
